newsitem.title: USA: Banks earned record $52.4 billion in 1996 - FDIC.
newsitem.headline: Banks earned record $52.4 billion in 1996 - FDIC.

text.p: Commercial banks earned a record $52.4 billion in 1996, up seven percent from the previous record, set in 1995, of $48.7 billion, Federal Deposit Insurance Corp said on Thursday.
Banks would have earned $650 million more but had to make one-time payments to help replenish the federal insurance fund for savings institutions, the FDIC said.
Savings institutions had net income of $7 billion for 1996, a drop of $611 million from the previous year. The one-time payments reduced savings earnings by $2.2 billion.
Only six federally-insured institutions failed in 1996, FDIC said, the lowest total since 1972 when just five banks and savings institutions failed.
But the news was not all good, FDIC said. Banks had to write off a net $9.5 billion on credit card loans, an increase of almost 40 percent from 1995.

At the same time, banks continued to increase their lending on credit cards. Loans and unused commitments increased more than $92 billion, or six percent, in the fourth quarter to a total of $1.57 trillion, FDIC said.
FDIC chairman Ricki Helfer termed the statistics "worrisome."

"As large as these number are, we believe they understate the exposure of banks to risk in credit card lending because they do not fully account for potential claims that could arise from continuing liabilities related to credit card loans that have been securitized," Helfer said.
But she added that industry appears strong enough to weather any problems. "Despite these concerns, the outlook for banking remains bright," Helfer said.
Commercial banks' average return on assets was 1.19 percent in 1996, just shy of the 1993 record of 1.20 percent and a slight increase from 1995's 1.17 percent, the FDIC said.
Non-interest income rose 13.5 percent, or $11.1 billion, to $93.6 billion in 1996. Interest income rose 5.6 percent, or $8.6 billion, to $162.8 billion.
